---
title: Glossary
---

We work across climate science, statistics, decision analysis, and engineering, and those fields use some of the same words differently. This page records how the group uses them. When you settle terminology with coauthors in a [paper contract](../guides/papers.qmd#paper-contract), start here.

::: {.callout-note}
## How Settled Are These Definitions?

They are working definitions for this group, and other fields may use the terms differently. Where a term is contested, the entry says so instead of picking one meaning. If you think an entry is wrong, please [say so](../contributing/index.qmd).
:::

## Kinds of Uncertainty

Deep uncertainty
:   The situation where the parties to a decision don't know, or can't agree on, the system model, the probability distributions of its inputs, or how to value the outcomes. It is different from a large amount of ordinary uncertainty: you can't write down an agreed probability distribution, which is why [expected-value methods are no longer the obvious tool](../guides/readinglist.qmd). The term also names a research community, decision-making under deep uncertainty.

Parametric uncertainty
:   Uncertainty about the values of a model's parameters, with its structure held fixed. Most analyses propagate this kind, because a Monte Carlo ensemble over a fixed model captures it.

Structural uncertainty
:   Uncertainty about the form of the model itself: which processes are represented, how they are coupled, and what is left out. Two group studies on the [reading list](../guides/readinglist.qmd) found it larger than parametric uncertainty in the systems they examined, so that analyses propagating only parametric uncertainty understated risk, often in the tail.

Model discrepancy
:   The systematic difference between a model's output and the system it represents, beyond observation error. It is a property of the model's structure, not random noise.

::: {.callout-warning}
## How Is Discrepancy Different From a Residual?

A residual is what is left over after fitting a model to data. Discrepancy is the claim that the model is wrong in a structured way. The difference has consequences for calibration: if you ignore discrepancy, the fitted parameters absorb the structural error, so their estimates tend to be biased and their uncertainty intervals too narrow.

Our own materials have not always kept the two apart, and the reading list includes Brynjarsdóttir and O'Hagan for this reason. Use "discrepancy" when you mean the structural difference.
:::

Epistemic and aleatory uncertainty
:   Epistemic uncertainty comes from lack of knowledge and can in principle be reduced by learning more; aleatory uncertainty is variability in the system itself, which can't. Where the boundary falls depends on the model and is often arguable, so treat the distinction as a modeling choice.

## Risk

Risk
:   Commonly broken into hazard, exposure, and vulnerability, which interact instead of simply multiplying. Which of the three contributes the most uncertainty depends on the analysis. Hosseini-Shakib et al. (2024, on the [reading list](../guides/readinglist.qmd)) found projected riverine flood risk most sensitive to hazard factors, while other group work has found that uncertainty in how buildings are described and valued can be large enough to change which management option looks best.

Hazard
:   The physical event and its characteristics over space and time: the flood, the storm surge, the heat wave.

Exposure
:   What is in harm's way: assets, people, infrastructure.

Vulnerability
:   How much damage exposed assets take for a given hazard. Depth-damage functions are the standard example.

::: {.callout-note}
## Two Uses of "Hazard"

In careful use, hazard is one of the three parts of risk. In looser use, including in some of our own older papers, it stands for the whole risk estimate. Check which meaning a paper intends before assuming the narrow one.
:::

## Models and Their Evaluation

Exploratory modeling
:   Using ensembles of plausible models to map what *could* happen and which possibilities matter, instead of treating one model as a stand-in for the system and asking what *will* happen. The alternative is called consolidative modeling. Exploratory modeling is the group's basic epistemic stance, and [Bankes](../guides/readinglist.qmd) is the reading-list entry that explains it.

Emulator
:   A fast statistical approximation of an expensive model (also called a surrogate), fitted to a sample of the model's runs. Emulators are used when the full model is too slow for the number of evaluations an analysis needs.

Sensitivity analysis
:   Attributing the variation in a model's output to variation in its inputs. Global sensitivity analysis varies inputs across their full ranges at the same time; local analysis perturbs them around one point. For nonlinear models with interactions, which describes many of ours, local results can be badly misleading. The [MSD uncertainty eBook](https://uc-ebook.org) is the group's practical reference.

Calibration
:   Estimating model parameters from observations.

::: {.callout-warning}
## Two Senses of Verification and Validation

In the modeling sense, Oreskes et al. (on the reading list) argue that verification and validation of numerical models of natural systems are impossible, because natural systems are never closed and model results are never unique. In their words, models "can be confirmed by the demonstration of agreement between observation and prediction, but confirmation is inherently partial," and they "can only be evaluated in relative terms."

In the software sense used in [Coding Best Practices](../guides/best-practices.qmd), "validation" means unit testing and "verified" means reviewed and merged.

Both senses appear in this manual. Check which one is meant, and make it clear when you write.
:::

## Projections and Scenarios

Projection
:   A conditional statement of what the model says follows *given* a scenario. It is not a forecast, because it holds only under the scenario's assumptions.

Prediction
:   An unconditional claim about what will happen. We rarely make them.

Scenario
:   A coherent, internally consistent description of a possible future, used as an input assumption. A scenario is not a probability statement, and SSPs and RCPs are not ranked by likelihood.

State of the world (SOW)
:   One fully specified combination of uncertain factors, and the unit of a large ensemble. An analysis over tens of thousands of SOWs asks which combinations produce outcomes we care about, not which combination is most likely.

## Decision-Making

Robustness
:   How well a strategy performs across a wide range of futures, as opposed to how well it performs in expectation. Robust strategies usually give up some performance in the most likely future to avoid failing badly in others.

Resilience
:   The capacity of a system to absorb a disturbance and recover its function. Resilience is a property of the system; robustness is a property of a strategy.

Reliability
:   In our energy systems work, the technical sense: the probability that a system meets demand under specified conditions.

Regret
:   The difference between a strategy's outcome and the best outcome that could have been achieved if the future had been known. Minimizing the maximum regret is one decision criterion under deep uncertainty. The ordinary English word also appears in our writing, so check which is meant.

Rival framings
:   The observation that how a decision problem is formulated (which objectives, which constraints, whose outcomes count) shapes the answer as much as the analysis does, and that comparing formulations is itself informative.

## Extremes

Return level
:   The value expected to be exceeded once, on average, over a given period. The 100-year return level is the flood level exceeded on average once per century.

Return period
:   The inverse: the average time between exceedances. "The 100-year flood" is often read as a flood that happens once a century, which is wrong in two ways: the 100 years is a long-run average, and under nonstationarity the underlying distribution itself changes over time.

Block maxima and peaks over threshold
:   The two standard approaches to extreme value analysis, which fit either the maximum in each block of time (usually a year) or every exceedance above a threshold. The second uses more of the data, but its results can depend strongly on the threshold chosen.

## Group Tools and Conventions

Meta-repository
:   A repository holding one paper's analysis, which points to released versions of the models and data it uses instead of containing them. See [git and GitHub](programming/git.qmd#setting-up-project-repositories).

Paper contract
:   A document agreed early in a project that records the author line, expected contributions, research questions, hypotheses, and submission plan. See [Paper Writing](../guides/papers.qmd#paper-contract).

BRICK
:   Building blocks for Relevant Ice and Climate Knowledge, a semi-empirical sea-level model used across the group's coastal work and implemented in the Mimi framework as `MimiBRICK.jl`.

UNSAFE
:   UNcertain Structure And Fragility Ensemble, the group's framework for estimating property-level flood risk under uncertainty in exposure and vulnerability.

MSD
:   MultiSector Dynamics, the research program studying how human and Earth systems evolve together across sectors. Much of the group's uncertainty work is part of this community.

## Acronyms

Several of these appear in group materials without being spelled out. Please spell them out at first use.

| Acronym | Meaning |
|---|---|
| ABC | Approximate Bayesian Computation |
| CMIP | Coupled Model Intercomparison Project |
| DDF | Depth-Damage Function |
| GCM | General Circulation Model |
| GEV | Generalized Extreme Value (distribution) |
| GSA | Global Sensitivity Analysis |
| IAM | Integrated Assessment Model |
| IRB | Institutional Review Board |
| MCMC | Markov chain Monte Carlo |
| MSD | MultiSector Dynamics |
| POT / GP | Peaks Over Threshold / Generalized Pareto |
| RCP | Representative Concentration Pathway |
| RDM | Robust Decision Making |
| SOW | State Of the World |
| SSP | Shared Socioeconomic Pathway |
| UQ | Uncertainty Quantification |

## Missing an Entry?

If you come across a term that should be here, please add it. Entries that record a disagreement or an ambiguity are more useful than ones that record a definition everyone already shares.
